name: Neovim
summary: A terminal editor whose core owns mutable buffer and UI state while an event loop coordinates jobs, timers, input, embedded Lua execution, and MessagePack-RPC clients.

features.name: Event-driven editor core
features.description: The fixed source initializes a main event loop, channels, timers, processes, and UI state, then polls events as part of the editor lifecycle. Editor operations therefore advance through shared mutable state in response to asynchronous input and scheduled work.
benefits: Unifies terminal input, jobs, timers, and UI activity under one coordination model
Allows external processes and remote UIs to progress without blocking every editor operation
costs: Callbacks and queued events make ordering and reentrancy part of correctness
Long-running synchronous work can delay unrelated editor activity

features.name: MessagePack-RPC channel boundary
features.description: Neovim exposes API calls and notifications through RPC channels, including embedded stdio mode and socket-connected clients. The fixed source initializes channel and MessagePack-RPC components alongside the editor core.
benefits: Permits UIs, plugins, and other clients to drive the same editor API
Separates transport framing from editor state transitions
costs: Transport failures and asynchronous responses must be represented at the client boundary
API compatibility and channel lifecycle become integration contracts

features.name: Embedded Lua script boundary
features.description: The source initializes an embedded Lua interpreter and loads plugins through startup configuration; the API documentation describes Lua access to editor state and namespaced APIs. This creates a host-controlled scripting boundary over buffers, commands, events, and UI operations.
benefits: Makes editor behavior programmable without changing the core executable
Exposes structured editor state to plugins through documented APIs
costs: Plugin behavior shares the editor lifecycle and can affect responsiveness
Configuration, API compatibility, and plugin ordering add operational complexity

mathematical_views.question: How do input, RPC messages, timers, process events, callbacks, and buffer/UI mutations advance Neovim state?
assumptions: Editor state includes buffers, windows, clients, jobs, and pending events
The event loop is modeled as selecting and dispatching enabled transitions
The view abstracts terminal timing, operating-system scheduling, and exact callback queues

mathematical_views.question: Which clients and scripts can observe or mutate editor state through API calls and notifications?
assumptions: Editor state is a central resource vertex and channels/plugins are boundary vertices
Edges represent documented requests, notifications, callbacks, or Lua API calls
The graph describes reachability and does not imply that every path is safe, synchronous, or authorized

benefits: One loop coordinates interactive and asynchronous work
costs: Scheduling, callback ordering, and responsiveness become coupled

benefits: Remote and embedded clients can share a structured API
costs: Transport and protocol lifecycle failures cross the editor boundary

benefits: Plugins extend editor behavior through host APIs
costs: Extension behavior and compatibility increase lifecycle complexity
